source: Prakken (2020) Historical overview of formal argumentation
finding: Toulmin (1958) attacked the classic view that every good argument must be deductively valid. He said that outside mathematics an argument is valid if it survives criticism in a properly conducted dispute. This is the root of the field.
numbers: Toulmin scheme: 6 elements (claim, data, warrant, backing, qualifier, rebuttal).
limits: Toulmin gave a pictorial scheme, not a formal logic. Influence on AI was modest until Pollock and Dung formalised the idea.
agent_relevance: Our agent should treat a conclusion as a claim that stays open to challenge, with explicit warrant and exception slots, not as a closed deduction.

source: Bench-Capon, Atkinson, Bex, Prakken, Verheij (2024) Computational Models of Legal Argument (handbook chapter)
finding: Toulmin's scheme adds backing, qualifier and rebuttal to premise-rule-conclusion. It shows three ways to defeat an argument: the rule is unfounded, the rule does not apply here, or a stronger counter-argument exists. Walton's more flexible schemes later replaced it in AI and law.
numbers: 6 elements; qualifiers such as certainly, probably, possibly, typically, usually.
limits: Qualifier words are informal; no calculus for combining them.
agent_relevance: A cheap schema slot: every claim carries a warrant, a backing, a qualifier and an explicit 'unless' list. The unless list is the exception check.

source: Prakken (2020) Historical overview of formal argumentation
finding: Pollock (1987) introduced the defeasible reason (prima facie reason) and two kinds of defeater. A rebutting defeater supports the opposite conclusion. An undercutting defeater attacks the inference itself without supporting any opposite conclusion (red light makes 'looks red' no reason for 'is red'). Pollock also formalised defeasible reasons for perception, memory, induction, the statistical syllogism and temporal persistence.
numbers: Penguin example: rebut. Red-illumination example: undercut. Pollock says he first developed the idea in 1979.
limits: Pollock's 1995 semantics is shown to be an instance of Dung's grounded semantics; his 1994 version relates to preferred semantics.
agent_relevance: Two different challenge operators for the agent: 'your conclusion is wrong' versus 'your reason does not apply here'. Undercutting is the one a model tends to skip.

source: Prakken (2020) Historical overview of formal argumentation
finding: Dung (1995) showed argument evaluation needs only two primitives: arguments and an attack relation. Semantics (admissible, complete, preferred, stable, grounded) then pick coherent sets of arguments that defend themselves. He also showed default logic, Pollock's system, logic-programming semantics and cooperative game theory share this pattern.
numbers: Grounded extension is unique and contained in every other extension. Every stable extension is preferred, not vice versa. All extension types are complete.
limits: The paper is now cited almost only for the abstract part. Structure of arguments and source of attack are left open.
agent_relevance: The grounded status is a code-checkable, deterministic rule for which claims survive. The program can compute it; the model only supplies arguments and attacks.

source: Prakken and Vreeswijk (2002) Logics for Defeasible Argumentation (Handbook of Philosophical Logic chapter)
finding: Survey of the field. Argument-based logics model defeasible reasoning as argument, counter-argument, attack and defeat. It reviews Pollock, Dung and Bondarenko et al., Nute's defeasible logic, Reiter default logic and priorities. It notes that proving new facts without rejecting earlier ones can reverse a legal outcome, which classical logic cannot explain.
numbers: Chapter sections on Dung, Pollock and Nute's Defeasible Logic; rebutting, undercutting and assumption attack.
limits: Written 2002; before ASPIC+ and before LLMs.
agent_relevance: Gives the vocabulary for the agent's challenge step: rebut, undercut, undermine.

source: Prakken (2010) An abstract framework for argumentation with structured arguments (ASPIC+)
finding: ASPIC+ builds arguments as inference trees from strict and defeasible rules. This gives three attacks: on a premise (undermining), on a conclusion (rebutting), on an inference (undercutting). Preferences resolve undermining and rebutting; undercutting always succeeds. The result is a Dung framework. Rationality postulates are proven, and assumption-based argumentation and DefLog are shown to be special cases.
numbers: 3 attack types; 3 defeat types; postulates proven under stated conditions.
limits: Needs a reasonable preference ordering and consistent axioms; nature of rules left open.
agent_relevance: Best available blueprint for turning a defeasible rule base into a checkable program. The program computes defeat; the model supplies rules.

source: Modgil and Prakken (2014) The ASPIC+ framework for structured argumentation: a tutorial
finding: Four rationality postulates (sub-argument closure, closure under strict rules, direct consistency, indirect consistency) hold for complete extensions only if strict rules are closed under transposition or contraposition, axioms are consistent, and the ordering is reasonable. Allowing attacks on strict conclusions breaks them.
numbers: 4 postulates (Caminada and Amgoud 2007). Counterexample: if attacks on strict conclusions were allowed, {A1,A2,B1,B2} is stable and preferred yet violates closure and indirect consistency.
limits: Postulates are conditional. Naive preference-based attack frameworks violate them.
agent_relevance: Guardrail idea: never let a preference override a certain conclusion, and never accept a set of conclusions that jointly contradict. Both are code-checkable.

source: Modgil and Prakken (2014) ASPIC+ tutorial, last-link vs weakest-link (Examples 3.25 and 3.26)
finding: Which argument wins depends on the ordering rule. For legal rules (snoring counts as misbehaving; professors may not be denied library access) last-link seems right: the conflict does not weaken the earlier step. For empirical generalisations (born in Scotland, likes whisky, versus fitness lover) weakest-link seems right: uncertainty in early steps weakens the whole argument.
numbers: Two worked examples; intuitions argued, not tested with participants.
limits: Intuition-based; no human data in the tutorial.
agent_relevance: The agent should know whether it weighs norms (last link) or empirical claims (weakest link). A wrong choice flips the verdict.

source: Gordon, Prakken, Walton (2007) The Carneades model of argument and burden of proof
finding: Carneades evaluates an argument graph with a proof standard per statement. The burden of proof can be assigned to each premise separately and can change as the dialogue moves. Burden of production and burden of persuasion are handled separately. Critical questions of argument schemes are modelled as ways to shift the burden.
numbers: Three standards defined formally: scintilla of evidence (SE), best argument (BA), dialectical validity (DV); a complement is derived by swapping pro and con.
quote: burden of production and burden of persuasion can be handled separately
limits: Does not model preponderance of evidence or beyond reasonable doubt precisely; authors list this as future work.
agent_relevance: Gives the agent a table: for each claim, who must show what, and how strong the support must be. Different claims can need different standards.

source: Gordon, Prakken, Walton (2007) Carneades: legal definitions of the burdens
finding: Legal doctrine: failing the burden of persuasion means the issue is decided against that party, and this burden does not shift. Burden of production is the liability to an adverse ruling if no evidence is given. The plaintiff usually carries production for operative facts, the defendant for exceptions. In criminal law the prosecution carries persuasion against exceptions such as self-defence.
numbers: Sources cited: Wigmore, McCormick on Evidence, Park-Leonard-Goldberg. Degrees named: more likely than not; beyond reasonable doubt.
limits: Description of common-law practice; civil-law systems treat the split implicitly.
agent_relevance: Record for each exception who must raise it and who must refute it. Raising an exception is cheap; defeating it is not.

source: Prakken and Sartor (2009) A logical analysis of burdens of proof
finding: Burden of proof is analysed as part of rational thinking, fit for logics of defeasible argumentation. Three burdens: production (never shifts once met), persuasion (fixed by law, can be spread over both parties), and tactical (not set by law; moves back and forth depending on who would now lose if the case ended). Murder example: prosecution proves killing and intent; defence produces self-defence; prosecution now has a tactical burden.
numbers: 3 burdens; common-law and civil-law systems compared (Dutch and Italian law put persuasion for some exceptions on the defendant).
quote: the burden of production never shifts since once fulfilled it is disregarded
limits: Legal allocation differs by system. Courts keep discretion on fairness grounds.
agent_relevance: A tactical-burden check: after each round ask who loses if we stopped now. If we do, add evidence. Code can compute this with a grounded-status check.

source: Prakken and Sartor (2007) Formalising arguments about the burden of persuasion (ICAIL)
finding: The 1996 Prakken-Sartor system is reinterpreted as a system of burdens of persuasion. The 2001 system is extended so allocation of the burden can itself be argued over inside the logic, and can be spread over both sides. Applied to real legal cases.
numbers: No numbers; formal system with worked cases.
limits: Allocation of burdens is treated as logically contestable, but rules for who decides are not given.
agent_relevance: The agent may need to argue about which side carries the burden before arguing the facts. Treat that as its own step.

source: Bench-Capon et al. (2024) chapter, the case-based branch (HYPO, CATO)
finding: Early AI and law split into rule-based logic programming (British Nationality Act) and case-based HYPO. HYPO modelled argument as plies: cite a case, respond by distinguishing or counter-citing, rebut. Rules with exceptions gave defeasibility; precedents gave dimensions.
numbers: HYPO (Rissland and Ashley 1987); CATO (Aleven 1997) as successor.
limits: Case-based side belongs to the analogy and precedent subfield; only noted here.
agent_relevance: Defeasible rules cover statutes; analogy and precedent cover cases. The agent needs both.

source: Kazemi et al. (2023) BoardgameQA: natural language reasoning with contradictory information
finding: Dataset where rules conflict and a preference order (for example recency) decides which rule wins; labels are proved, disproved or unknown. Few-shot prompting of large LMs did poorly on conflict resolution; fine-tuned models did better. Conflict resolution does not surface out of the box.
numbers: Per variant: 1000 train, 500 validation, 1000 test, balanced labels, majority baseline 33%. Models: BERT, T5 1.1 XXL, prompt-tuned PaLM 62B, few-shot PaLM 62B and 540B with CoT, FLAN-PaLM 540B. Depths 1 to 3.
quote: LMs perform poorly when reasoning with conflicting sources
limits: Accuracy values appear only in figures; not recoverable from text. Synthetic story language. 2023 models.
agent_relevance: Direct evidence that a plain model with chain of thought does not reliably honour rule priority. A program that applies priorities is safer.

source: Kazemi et al. (2023) BoardgameQA: effect of conflict amount and type
finding: Accuracy fell as the share of examples with conflicts rose. BERT was above random for no-conflict and low-conflict data but near random for medium and high conflict. Type 2 conflicts (the losing rule's body must be shown unprovable) were harder than Type 1 (ignore the losing rule).
numbers: Conflict probability set to 0.0, 0.2, 0.5, 0.8.
limits: Numbers in figures only.
agent_relevance: Difficulty lies in showing an exception's condition fails, not in noticing the exception. The agent should check exception conditions explicitly.

source: Kazemi et al. (2023) BoardgameQA: proofs, distractors, missing information
finding: Models often wrote wrong proofs even when labels were right; few-shot models did poorly on conflict-resolution F1 while tuned models did much better. More distractor facts hurt few-shot models monotonically. At higher depths, prompt-tuned models guessed proved or disproved even when the true label was unknown.
numbers: Manual proof check on 50 sampled examples per model at depth 2. Prompt-tuned model predicted unknown 268 times at depth 1 but only 2 times at depth 2.
limits: A few distractors helped slightly in some settings; amount of required knowledge barely changed few-shot results.
agent_relevance: Over-commitment under missing information is the main danger; 'unknown' needs a code-checked route rather than a model decision.

source: Tachmazidis, Batsakis, Antoniou (2024) Benchmarking defeasible reasoning with LLMs
finding: GPT-4o with step-by-step prompts was tested on 8 theories adapted from the defeasible-logic benchmark of Maher et al. (2001), each in four settings (target true or false, statements random or ordered). Chains, circles and hierarchies came out right; conflicts without priority did not.
numbers: 8 theories x 4 settings = 32 runs. levels-(5) wrong in all 4 settings; levels(5) wrong in 2 of 4; dag(3,2) wrong in 1 of 4; other cells correct.
quote: ChatGPT seems to adopt the closed-world assumption
limits: Tiny sample, single model, manual reading of chats, no repeats. Authors call it first steps.
agent_relevance: GPT-4o seems to assume a closed world, invents facts, and does not leave a conclusion open when rules conflict without priority. The agent needs an explicit 'neither provable' output.

source: Kirkpatrick and Sterken (2025) Generics and default reasoning in LLMs
finding: 28 LLMs were tested on 20 defeasible patterns with generics (Birds fly). Top models did very well zero-shot; many models failed to separate defeasible from deductive inference or treated generics as universals.
numbers: Zero-shot, temperature 0: Claude 3 Opus and Claude 3.5 Sonnet 96%+; GPT-4 (0613) 96%; GPT-4 Turbo (2024-04-09) 93%; Gemma 2 9B 92%; 11 models 78-89%; 7 near chance; 3 below chance. Chance is 50%.
limits: Scored against philosophers' expert judgements; non-monotonic size trends (Gemma 2 9B beat 27B; Gemini 1.5 Flash beat Pro).
agent_relevance: Frontier models handle simple defaults. The weak spot is the exception-permitting nature of generics and prompt wording, not basic recall.

source: Kirkpatrick and Sterken (2025): chain-of-thought degrades default reasoning
finding: Chain-of-thought often hurt. For models above 75% zero-shot, mean accuracy drop was 11.14 points (SD 15.74). Claude 3 Sonnet fell more than 16 points, GPT-4 (0613) more than 12. GPT-4o improved (+17.44 May version, +4.98 August version). Code Llama 34B went from 6.48% to above 62%. Four error patterns: generic read as universal; defeasible versus deductive confusion; overly statistical; step-consistent but wrong conclusion.
numbers: Error analysis on 3 models with CoT deltas -0.33 (Claude 3.5 Sonnet), -12.62 (GPT-4 0613), -18.77 (Gemini 1.5 Flash).
limits: Authors offer overthinking and competence-gap explanations; not tested against each other.
agent_relevance: Free-form chain of thought can turn a defeasible rule into a universal. Prefer a structured exception check over open reasoning for default rules.

source: Kirkpatrick and Sterken (2025): few-shot, wording, irrelevance
finding: Few-shot helped weak models (Llama 2 Chat 7B +28.74, Claude 3 Haiku +25.08, GPT-4o May +16.27) but hurt Claude 3 Opus (-6.81). Alternative wordings of one pattern correlated 0.99 for minor changes but 0.43 to 0.54 for others, and -0.05 for one. Most strong models ignored irrelevant facts and defaults. Argument length and negation did not systematically lower accuracy of models above 90%.
limits: Single prompt battery; philosophical items, not legal text.
agent_relevance: Wording sensitivity means one phrasing of an exception check is not enough; run several and compare.

source: Li, Fang, Chen, Li, Liao (2025) Enhancing conflict resolution in language models via abstract argumentation
finding: Zero-shot chain-of-thought LLMs fail at computing Dung semantics. Fine-tuning Qwen2.5-7B and Llama3-8B on step-by-step explanations lifts grounded-extension accuracy to about 0.95-0.97 and generalises to larger graphs better than training on answers only.
numbers: Grounded-extension accuracy: Llama3-8B 0.18, Llama3-70B 0.37, Qwen2.5-7B 0.31, Qwen2.5-72B 0.48, GPT-3.5 0.15, GPT-4o 0.54; Qwen2.5-SFT 0.97, Llama3-SFT 0.95. Models trained without explanations sometimes fell to 30% beyond 25 arguments.
limits: Abstract frameworks only, no natural-language arguments. Table text was garbled in extraction; first column read as grounded accuracy.
agent_relevance: Computing who wins from an attack graph is better done by code than by a model, even a large one. Give the program the graph.

source: Li et al. (2025): explanation ablation and conflict-resolving ability
finding: Training with full explanations improved generalisation over masked explanations or result-only steps. Conflict-resolving scores rose from about 0.4-0.5 before training to near 1.0 after.
numbers: Llama3-8B scored 0.51, 0.42, 0.45, 0.48 on four conflict-resolving measures before training; Qwen2.5-SFT reached 1.00 and 0.95 under preferred semantics; Llama3-SFT 1.00 and 0.99 under complete.
limits: Ablation table columns were hard to map after text extraction; only the direction (full explanation best) is used.
agent_relevance: If we ever fine-tune, train on worked derivations, not answers. In the scaffold, show the derivation step by step.

source: Batzoglou (2026) ABD: default-exception abduction in finite first-order worlds
finding: Solver-checkable benchmark: given a default theory and observations that violate it, the model must write a first-order abnormality rule (the exceptions) that restores consistency with as few exceptions as possible. Three regimes: full, partial (existential completion), skeptical (universal completion). Eleven frontier LLMs, 600 instances, seven default theories.
numbers: Opus-4.6 prompt validity 100/98/99/99 across four reported groups; Gemini-3.1 99/97/96/96. Among strong models, prompt-set gaps of 1 to 1.5 extra exceptions per world remain; valid-formula size in the low teens (AST 12.4 for Opus-4.6 in the first group). Temperature 0.1.
limits: Synthetic finite worlds; no natural language. Gap measured only on valid formulas.
agent_relevance: Models write valid exceptions but too many of them (marking everything abnormal is always valid). Parsimony needs a code check.

source: Batzoglou (2026) ABD: generalisation to holdout worlds
finding: On fresh holdout worlds (5 per instance) the main failure in the full and partial regimes is parsimony inflation (gaps roughly double). In the skeptical regime it is validity brittleness: rules that fit the prompt worlds often fail on holdouts. GPT-5.4 had the lowest gap but with huge formulas and lower validity.
numbers: 5 holdout worlds per instance; gaps roughly double on holdouts; 95% bootstrap intervals reported.
limits: Holdout set not adversarially hardened. Provider-default reasoning settings.
agent_relevance: A repaired exception rule must be re-tested on unseen cases before the agent trusts it. This fits the held-out check in the schema.

source: Reiter (1980), McCarthy (1980), Gelfond and Lifschitz (1988): classical nonmonotonic formalisms, as described in Batzoglou (2026) and Prakken (2020)
finding: Default logic, circumscription and stable-model semantics treat exceptions as a feature, not a bug. Dung (1995) showed they share structure with argumentation semantics. Reiter's default logic underlies the typically-style rules in the LLM benchmarks above.
numbers: Three formalisms named; no new numbers.
limits: Read only through two secondary sources; the original papers were not opened.
agent_relevance: Borrow the abnormality-predicate trick: every default carries an explicit unless-Ab condition that is checked, not assumed false.

source: Ford (2005) Human nonmonotonic reasoning: the importance of seeing the logical strength of arguments (Synthese)
finding: Search-snippet abstract only. Participants found default reasoning hard. Specificity, long treated as the key to correct defeasible conclusions, was irrelevant on some problems where 'can't tell' would be expected, yet people still reached reasoned conclusions by comparing the logical consequences of the competing arguments.
numbers: No sample sizes read.
limits: Not opened. Snippet from a search result; treat as a lead.
agent_relevance: Human data suggest people do not apply specificity as a rule. Do not assume formal priority rules match human defaults.

source: Ford and Billington (2000) Strategies in human nonmonotonic reasoning (Computational Intelligence 16:446-468)
finding: Earlier human study of nonmonotonic reasoning and specificity. Only bibliographic data seen, via a search result and the reference list of Tachmazidis et al. (2024).
numbers: Not read.
limits: Not opened; no results seen. Needs follow-up.
agent_relevance: Lead for human baselines on specificity and conflicting defaults.

source: Hahn and Oaksford (2007) The burden of proof and its role in argumentation (Argumentation 21:39-61)
finding: Search-result description only. Argues burden of proof has been extended from law into argumentation studies too broadly, and links it to argument from ignorance, argument strength and decision-theoretic standards of proof.
numbers: Not read.
limits: Not opened; abstract-level only.
agent_relevance: Lead: a Bayesian reading of burden and strength could give the agent graded standards instead of three crisp ones.

source: Toulmin (1958) The Uses of Argument
finding: The book itself was not opened. Two opened reviews report: a warrant licenses the step from data to claim, is itself defeasible, and an argument is valid if it withstands criticism in a properly conducted dispute.
numbers: Not applicable.
limits: Book not opened; description taken from two opened secondary sources.
agent_relevance: Use the six-part scheme only via secondary sources for now.
